canonical_statement: The ancillary TIMI-5 analysis evaluated mechanisms of thrombin formation, the balance of coagulation and fibrinogenolysis during rt-PA treatment, and whether hemostatic markers predicted clinical events in acute myocardial infarction.

TIMI-5 enrolled patients with at least 30 minutes of chest pain who presented within 6 hours of symptom onset and had ST-segment elevation of at least 0.1 mV in at least 2 contiguous leads or new left bundle branch block.

A second hirudin regimen used a 0.1 mg/kg intravenous bolus followed by 0.1 mg/kg/h infusion in 33 patients.
A third hirudin regimen used a 0.3 mg/kg intravenous bolus followed by 0.1 mg/kg/h infusion in 29 patients.
A fourth hirudin regimen used a 0.6 mg/kg intravenous bolus followed by 0.2 mg/kg/h infusion in 50 patients.
After the study-drug bolus, all patients received front-loaded alteplase: 15 mg intravenous bolus, 0.75 mg/kg (maximum 50 mg) over 30 minutes, then 0.50 mg/kg (maximum 35 mg) over 60 minutes.

canonical_statement: Coronary arteriography was performed at 90 minutes and again 18 to 36 hours after therapy initiation, with TIMI perfusion grades assigned by the Angiographic Core Laboratory.
PTCA could be performed at the attending cardiologist's discretion for TIMI grade 0 or 1 flow at 120 minutes; hirudin-treated patients undergoing PTCA were switched to heparin.

More heparin-treated than hirudin-treated patients underwent PTCA overall (50% vs 32%; p=0.006), but this difference was not present before 24 hours and rescue PTCA within 24 hours was similar between treatment groups.
Blood for hemostatic markers was collected before antithrombotic therapy and at 1, 12, and 24 hours after treatment initiation.
Samples were collected with EDTA, aprotinin, and PPACK, kept on ice, immediately centrifuged, stored at -70 C, and hemostatic markers were analyzed blinded to treatment.
Plasma fibrinopeptide A was measured by radioimmunoassay; the laboratory upper limit of normal was approximately 2 micrograms/L.
Prothrombin fragment 1.2 was measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay; control values were 0.21 to 2.78 nM.
Thrombin-antithrombin III complexes were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay; normal values were 1.5 to 3 micrograms/L.
Plasma Bbeta1-42 was measured after ethanol precipitation to remove fibrinogen, fibrin, and fibrin(ogen) degradation products; normal values were 4.5 to 5.9 nM (27 to 35.4 micrograms/L).

Poor-quality samples and spurious elevations were excluded by prespecified criteria; FPA values at least 250 micrograms/L were considered spurious, and repeated poor-quality values could exclude all data for a marker in an individual patient.

Because marker distributions were highly skewed, analyses used log10-transformed values and tertiles; repeated-measures ANOVA, t tests, chi-square tests, correlations, and stepwise logistic regression were used.
Final multivariable models included the hemostatic marker, treatment group, age, and gender after exploratory assessment of potential confounders.
Reported p values were not adjusted for multiple testing, and the authors explicitly instructed readers to interpret the analyses as exploratory.
At baseline before antithrombotic therapy, mean Fibrinopeptide A was 47.34 micrograms/L (SD 51.28; n=138; listed normal range <=2 micrograms/L).

canonical_statement: Baseline hemostatic marker levels did not differ significantly by randomized treatment group.

Mean FPA declined over time overall (p<0.0001); the decline was not statistically significant in heparin-treated patients (p=0.13) but was significant in hirudin-treated patients (p<0.0001), with no significant between-treatment difference for FPA.

TAT levels were markedly divergent at 1 hour, remaining elevated in heparin-treated patients while falling to minimal values in hirudin-treated patients, but repeated-measures analysis found no significant change over time or significant difference between treatment groups.

Mean F1.2 rose initially at 1 hour and then fell over 12 hours (p<0.02), with similar overall trajectories between treatment groups (p=0.19); the highest hirudin dose showed a greater decline than the lowest hirudin dose (p=0.02) and heparin (p=0.03).
Mean Bbeta1-42 increased sharply at 1 hour and returned to baseline by 12 hours (p<0.0001), with similar changes in heparin- and hirudin-treated patients.
Patients who died had significantly higher 1-hour FPA levels than survivors (p=0.045).
Patients who died had significantly higher 1-hour TAT levels than survivors (p=0.0092).
TIMI grade 0 or 1 flow at 90 minutes was associated with higher F1.2 levels at 1 hour (p=0.048).
TIMI grade 0 or 1 flow at 90 minutes was associated with higher FPA levels at 12 hours (p=0.017).
TIMI grade 0 or 1 flow at 90 minutes was associated with higher Bbeta1-42 levels at 12 hours (p=0.0013).
Patients with TIMI grade 0, 1, or 2 flow at 90 minutes had higher 1-hour FPA levels than patients with TIMI grade 3 flow (p=0.024).
Patients with TIMI grade 0, 1, or 2 flow at 90 minutes had higher 1-hour TAT levels than patients with TIMI grade 3 flow (p=0.020).
At the 18- to 36-hour angiogram, TIMI grade 0, 1, or 2 flow was associated with higher TAT levels at 24 hours (p=0.047).

For 12-hour FPA, the association with failure to achieve TIMI grade 2 or 3 reperfusion at 90 minutes was statistically significant in heparin-treated patients (p=0.026) but not in hirudin-treated patients (p=0.16).
Hemorrhagic events were associated with higher 1-hour levels of FPA (p=0.036), F1.2 (p=0.032), and TAT (p=0.029).
Patients with anterior myocardial infarction were increasingly represented in higher 1-hour FPA tertiles (p=0.019).
Patients classified as not low risk were increasingly represented in higher 1-hour FPA tertiles (p=0.027).
Women were increasingly represented in higher 12-hour TAT tertiles compared with men (p=0.025).
Patients with a history of hypertension were increasingly represented in higher 12-hour Bbeta1-42 tertiles (p=0.016).
Patients with a history of hypertension were increasingly represented in higher 12-hour F1.2 tertiles (p=0.0060).
Among hemorrhagic events, 85.4% occurred at instrumented sites and were temporally related to cardiac catheterization.

canonical_statement: FPA and TAT levels were significantly correlated at all four measurement time points (p<0.0001).
FPA and F1.2 levels at 24 hours were significantly correlated (p=0.0044).
TAT levels at 12 hours were significantly correlated with time to treatment (p=0.02).
The authors concluded that early markers of thrombin activity and generation may help predict death and failure to achieve reperfusion after thrombolytic therapy for acute myocardial infarction.
The authors concluded that late increases in Bbeta1-42, F1.2, and TAT may be predictive of recurrent ischemia.
The authors proposed that a high-risk hemostatic-marker profile at 1 hour might identify patients needing early catheterization and revascularization, contingent on validation in further studies.
Not every patient had marker measurements at all four time points; approximately 50% had valid measurements for each marker at every time point, limiting repeated-measures analyses.
Outcome analyses pooled patients across two antithrombotic drugs, including four hirudin doses, creating treatment heterogeneity that limited interpretation of biomarker-outcome associations.
The study performed many comparisons and the authors stated that the findings should be interpreted as suggestive rather than confirmatory.
The authors stated that the marker-outcome associations required confirmation in subsequent studies with larger numbers of patients in each treatment group.
